In this exercise, we'll continue our study of the bike sharing data, but we’re
starting to take off the training wheels: rather than using
pre-wrangled data, you’ll be doing some of the data wrangling yourself!

In this exercise you'll:

- *refine* your skills in creating reproducible documents (Quarto) and graphics (Plotly)
- *practice* grouping and aggregation functions in pandas
- *see* some ways to work with dates

## Getting Started

Create a folder for this exercise and create a new Quarto file in that folder named `ex05-bikeshare-wrangling.qmd`. Start with the usual setup code, given in the [course notes](../../notes/quarto.qmd#class-standards).

```{python}
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import plotly.express as px
pd.options.plotting.backend = "plotly"
```

## Load Data

We downloaded the data from the [Capital BikeShare program](https://www.capitalbikeshare.com/system-data). Note the license agreement there. We removed some columns of the data that we aren't using to reduce the size of the dataset you have to download.

::: {.callout collapse="true" title="Low-level wrangling code"}

If you're really curious, here's the code I used to make the parquet files. For this exercise, though, just used the provided data files.

```{python}
#| echo: true
import requests, zipfile, io, pathlib
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import glob

for year in [2011, 2012]:
    parquet_filename = f'data/bikeshare_{year}.parquet'
    if pathlib.Path(parquet_filename).exists():
        continue

    filenames = sorted(glob.glob(f"data/{year}*tripdata.csv"))
    if not filenames:
        print("Downloading", year, "data")
        url = f"https://s3.amazonaws.com/capitalbikeshare-data/{year}-capitalbikeshare-tripdata.zip"
        r = requests.get(url)
        z = zipfile.ZipFile(io.BytesIO(r.content))
        z.extractall("data")
        filenames = sorted(glob.glob(f"data/{year}*tripdata.csv"))

    df = pd.concat([
        pd.read_csv(filename,
        usecols=["Duration", "Start date", "Member type"], parse_dates=["Start date"])
        for filename in filenames], ignore_index=True)
    df.rename(columns={"Start date": "start_time", "Duration": "duration", "Member type": "rider_type"}, inplace=True)
    df.to_parquet(parquet_filename, index=False)
```

```{python}
# copy all of the parquet files into the ../../static/data/bikeshare folder
import shutil
all_parquet_files = glob.glob("data/*.parquet")
for filename in all_parquet_files:
    shutil.copy(filename, "../../static/data/bikeshare")
```

:::

We'll distribute the data for this exercise in a format called [Parquet](https://parquet.apache.org/), an efficient emerging standard for dataframe interchange. You can [read Parquet files with pandas](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/user_guide/io.html#parquet).

The data files are broken up by year. Here we read in the data for 2011, which is the first of the two years included in the dataset for previous exercises. **Download the data file [here](https://calvin-data-science.github.io/data202/data/bikeshare/bikeshare_2011.parquet)** and upload it to a `data` folder in your exercise folder.


```{python}
#| echo: true
rides_2011 = pd.read_parquet("data/bikeshare_2011.parquet")

rides = rides_2011
rides.info()
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="2012 data"}

Once you've finished with this exercise, you can use the following instructions to load the 2012 data also.

1. Download the data file [here](https://calvin-data-science.github.io/data202/data/bikeshare/bikeshare_2012.parquet)
2. Upload it to the `data` folder.
3. Use the following code to load it and concatenate it with the 2011 data (replacing the `rides = rides_2011` line above):

```{{python}}
rides_2012 = pd.read_parquet("data/bikeshare_2012.parquet")
rides = pd.concat([rides_2011, rides_2012], ignore_index=True)
```

:::

Each row is a *ride*. For each ride we're given the start time of the trip, its duration, and rider type.

::: {.column-margin}
According to the website:

Member Type – Indicates whether user was a "registered" member (Annual Member, 30-Day Member or Day Key Member) or a "casual" rider (Single Trip, 24-Hour Pass, 3-Day Pass or 5-Day Pass)
:::

## Part 2: Counting Rides By Day

Our goal is to create a dataframe like the one used in [Exercise 1](../01intro/ex01-warmup.qmd) that includes the number of rides in each day. We'll do this in two steps:


### Part 2A: Date Wrangling

The `start_time` column gives the timestamp (date and time) of when the ride started. We want to count the number of rides per day, so we need to extract the date from the timestamp. We can use the [`dt` accessor](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/user_guide/basics.html#basics-dt-accessors) to access the date part of the timestamp:

```{python}
#| echo: true
rides['date'] = rides['start_time'].dt.date
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="other dt accessors"}

The original dataframe also had columns for year, month, and day broken out. We won't need these (you can derive them all from `year`), but if you want them, you can use the [`dt` accessor](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/user_guide/basics.html#basics-dt-accessors) (short for "datetime"). For example: 


```python
rides['year'] = rides['start_time'].dt.year
```

:::

Check that the first few rows look like:

```{python}
rides.head(3)
```

(All of the code for this part has been provided for you above; you just need to include it in your document.)

### Part 2B: Counting

Count the number of rides for each date. Call the result `daily_rides`.

The first few rows of result should look like:

```{python}
daily_rides = (
    rides
    .groupby('date', as_index=False)
    .size()
    .rename(columns={'size': 'total_rides'})
)
daily_rides.head()
```

::: {.callout-tip}

To get the column to be named `total_rides` instead of `size`, you can either use an explicit aggregation, or rename the result using `.rename(columns={'size': 'total_rides'})`. Remember that by default, `DataFrame` methods return a *new* `DataFrame`, so you can just include the `rename` in the method chain.

:::

::: {.callout-note title="Data Types"}

The resulting `date` column is a `datetime.date` object, which is a Python object that represents a date (but not a time). pandas and Plotly don't handle this type of object well, so let's convert it to a `datetime` object. You can convert a column to a `datetime` object using `pd.to_datetime`:

```{python}
#| echo: true
daily_rides['date'] = pd.to_datetime(daily_rides['date'])
```

:::

Checklist:

- [ ] You created a `daily_rides` data frame that contains the number of rides per day.
- [ ] You converted the `date` column to a `datetime` object using the provided code.

## Part 3: Breaking down by rider type

Repeat Part 2, but now create a `daily_rides_by_type` data frame where you break down the counts by rider type, like we did in [Exercise 2](../01intro/ex02-bikeshare.qmd). For example:

```{python}
daily_rides_by_type = (
    rides
    .groupby(["date", "rider_type"], as_index=False)
    .size()
    .rename(columns={'size': 'rides'})
)
daily_rides_by_type.head()
```

Hint: you can group by multiple columns by passing a list of column names to `groupby`.

**Make sure you validate the shape of this data frame also**; there *is* a difference between the number of rows you expect and the number of rows you get. Fix the issue by using a `query` to remove a small number of rows.

```{python}
#| include: false
len(daily_rides_by_type) - 2 * len(daily_rides)
```

```{python}
daily_rides_by_type = (
    rides
    .query('rider_type != "Unknown"')
    .groupby(["date", "rider_type"], as_index=False)
    .size()
    .rename(columns={'size': 'rides'})
)
daily_rides_by_type['date'] = pd.to_datetime(daily_rides_by_type['date'])
```

Use the `daily_rides_by_type` data frame to recreate the plot from Exercise 2:

```{python}
(
  px.scatter(
    daily_rides_by_type,
    x="date", y="rides", color="rider_type",
    trendline="lowess",
    title="Number of Rides by Date, by Type of Rider",
    labels={"date": "Date", "rides": "Number of Rides", "rider_type": "Type of Rider"}
    )
    .update_traces(marker_size=3, marker_opacity=.5)
)
```

## Part 4: Breaking down by day of week

Recreate the "How does ridership vary over a typical week?" plot using this dataset.

::: {.callout-note title="Day of Week column"}

You'll need to add a column for the day of the week. Use the [`strftime` method](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.Series.dt.strftime.html) to get the name of the day of the week. We also need to convert the resulting column to a `Categorical` column so that Plotly will plot the days in the correct order and pandas will order the rows correctly when we group by day of week. Here's how I did it (admittedly with some help from GitHub Copilot!):

```{python}
#| echo: true
# Extract day of week
daily_rides_by_type['day_of_week'] = daily_rides_by_type['date'].dt.strftime("%a")
# Convert to an ordered Categorical
daily_rides_by_type['day_of_week'] = pd.Categorical(
    daily_rides_by_type['day_of_week'],
    categories=["Mon", "Tue", "Wed", "Thu", "Fri", "Sat", "Sun"],
    ordered=True
)
```

We're not going to study Categorical columns very much, but they're useful when dealing with qualitative data, especially when it's ordered. You can read more about them [here](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/user_guide/categorical.html).

:::

::: {.callout-note title="Other notes"}

- Omit the "Unknown" rider type (if you haven't already)
- If you're only using the 2011 rides, the specific values will be a bit different than what you saw in Exercise 2 because that also included 2012.
  You can add the 2012 data too if you like; see the notes at the beginning of the exercise.
:::

For reference, here's what I got when I used this dataset:

```{python}
#| echo: false
(
  px.box(
    daily_rides_by_type,
    x="day_of_week", y="rides", color="rider_type",
    labels={"day_of_week": "Day of Week", "rides": "Number of Rides", "rider_type": "Type of Rider"},
    title="Distribution of rides by day of week"
  )
)
```

Show the same summary as the plot above, but in tabular form.


```{python}
median_table = daily_rides_by_type.groupby(["day_of_week", "rider_type"], as_index=False).agg(median_rides=("rides", "median"))
median_table
```


```{python}
#| include: false
# pivot the rider_type column to get a table with one row per day of week
median_table.pivot(index="day_of_week", columns="rider_type", values="median_rides")
```
